Limitations with Negative Edge Weights and Bellman-Ford Dijkstra's algorithm strictly fails when a graph contains negative edge weights. The core greedy invariant assumes that once a vertex is extracted from the priority queue, its shortest path distance is permanently finalized and cannot be decreased by any subsequent paths. When negative edge weights exist, a longer path with a negative edge could yield a smaller total path weight after the vertex has already been settled, violating the optimality invariant. To solve the single-source shortest path problem on graphs with negative edge weights, the Bellman-Ford algorithm must be used instead. The Bellman-Ford algorithm runs in O(V * E) time and operates by relaxing all edges in the graph V - 1 times. Furthermore, Bellman-Ford can detect the presence of negative-weight cycles reachable from the source: if an additional relaxation step in the V-th iteration still decreases any vertex distance, a negative-weight cycle exists.

Database Management Systems: ACID Transactions and Concurrency Control A transaction in a database management system is a logical unit of database processing that includes one or more database access operations. Transactions must satisfy the ACID properties: 1. Atomicity: Either all operations of the transaction are executed and reflected in the database, or none are. Handled by the write-ahead logging (WAL) recovery manager. 2. Consistency: Execution of a transaction in isolation preserves database consistency invariants and integrity constraints. 3. Isolation: Even if multiple transactions execute concurrently, the system guarantees that for every pair of transactions T_i and T_j, it appears to T_i that either T_j finished execution before T_i started, or T_j started execution after T_i finished. 4. Durability: Once a transaction successfully commits, the updates made to the database persist even in the event of system crashes.

Coffman's Four Conditions for Deadlock A deadlock is a state in which each process in a set is waiting for an event that only another process in the set can cause. Edward G. Coffman Jr. formalized that a deadlock situation can arise if and only if all four of the following conditions hold simultaneously: 1. Mutual Exclusion: At least one resource must be held in a non-shareable mode (only one process can use the resource at a time). 2. Hold and Wait: A process must be currently holding at least one resource and requesting additional resources that are currently being held by other processes. 3. No Preemption: Resources cannot be forcibly preempted from a process; a resource can only be released voluntarily by the process holding it after completing its task. 4. Circular Wait: A closed chain of processes exists such that each process holds at least one resource needed by the next process in the chain (P_0 waits for resource held by P_1, ..., P_n waits for resource held by P_0).

Dynamic Programming and the 0/1 Knapsack Problem Dynamic programming is an algorithmic design paradigm based on the principle of optimality, where an optimal solution to an instance of a problem contains within it optimal solutions to subproblems. The two canonical properties required for dynamic programming to apply are optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems. In the 0/1 Knapsack Problem, we are given n items, each with a positive weight w_i and value v_i, and a knapsack of maximum capacity W. The objective is to select a subset of items to maximize total value without exceeding capacity W. Because each item can either be taken (1) or left behind (0), a simple greedy strategy based on value-to-weight ratio fails. The recurrence relation is defined over a 2D table DP[i][w]: if w_i <= w, DP[i][w] = max(DP[i-1][w], DP[i-1][w - w_i] + v_i); otherwise DP[i][w] = DP[i-1][w]. The time complexity is O(n * W), which is pseudo-polynomial in nature.

Operating Systems: Process Synchronization and Deadlocks In multiprogramming environments, concurrent access to shared data can lead to data inconsistency. A race condition arises when several processes access and manipulate the same data concurrently and the outcome depends on the particular order in which access takes place. The critical-section problem requires three structural conditions to be satisfied: 1. Mutual Exclusion: If process P_i is executing in its critical section, then no other processes can be executing in their critical sections. 2. Progress: If no process is executing in its critical section and there exist some processes that wish to enter their critical section, then only those processes not executing in their remainder sections can participate in deciding which will enter next. 3. Bounded Waiting: There must be a bound on the number of times other processes are allowed to enter their critical sections after a process has made a request to enter and before that request is granted.
